query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding ~0.1 wt.% boron during the melt synthesis of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA will improve its practical performance by enhancing grain boundary cohesion and refining the lamellar microstructure, thereby increasing resistance to creep, sustained mechanical loading, and corrosion under extreme temperature fluctuations.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure that currently exhibits a less than optimal strength–ductility balance and vulnerabilities (e.g., grain boundary decohesion) under service conditions.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled micro-alloying addition of approximately 0.1 wt.% boron during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: Tested under conditions of extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading at room temperature (creep conditions), and corrosive environments typical for aerospace fastener applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Boron is expected to preferentially segregate to grain and phase boundaries, lowering the grain boundary energy and suppressing unwanted grain boundary migration and decohesion. This segregation may also refine and stabilize the fine lamellar structure and retard creep-related deformation mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: By segregating to the grain and lamellar interfaces, boron reduces interfacial energy and acts as a barrier to dislocation movement and grain boundary sliding. This promotes improved load transfer and stability at the boundaries, leading to concurrent improvements in strength and ductility. Additionally, enhanced boundary chemistry may mitigate corrosion and creep by reducing segregation-induced weaknesses.
generation.predicted_outcome: An alloy with added boron is predicted to exhibit improved strength–ductility balance, reduced room-temperature creep, and enhanced corrosion resistance relative to the unmodified alloy. The improvements may include moderate increases in yield strength and ductility, although precise quantitative gains are uncertain.
generation.baseline: The current performance of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy without boron, which, despite its good strength and plasticity, falls short of the more rigorous industrial requirements for fastener applications in aerospace.
generation.boundary: The predicted improvements are expected within the context of the existing eutectic dual-phase lamellar microstructure and may only hold if the boron content is precisely controlled (~0.1 wt.%). Over-addition could lead to the formation of brittle boride phases, negating beneficial effects.
generation.uncertainty: The exact degree of performance improvement (e.g., precise percentage increases in strength or ductility) is uncertain and may depend on subtle interactions between boron segregation kinetics and the existing microstructure. There is also uncertainty on whether boron will form any deleterious phases at the alloy boundaries under processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA samples: one set with a controlled addition of ~0.1 wt.% boron and a control set without boron. Process both sets under identical conditions. Subject the samples to a series of mechanical tests (tensile, creep under long-term loading, and cyclic thermal fluctuation tests) and corrosion tests. Perform microstructural characterization (using SEM/TEM with elemental mapping) to examine grain boundary chemistry and phase stability.
measurements: Creep strain rate and time-to-failure under room-temperature loading
Corrosion rate in a controlled corrosive environment
Grain boundary composition analysis for evidence of boron segregation
Microstructural stability through high-temperature cycling experiments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-added samples do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in yield strength, ductility, creep resistance, and corrosion resistance, or if microstructural analysis shows the formation of brittle boride phases or no effective boron segregation at grain boundaries compared to the control samples, the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The properties of many metallic alloys are essentially related to the structure, morphology and chemical distribution of boundaries. In terms of atomic structure, the phase boundaries contained in eutectic dual-phase HEAs were supposed to be insufficient in prohibiting dislocations due to their semi-coherent nature, which is similar to those widely reported in NiAl dual-phase intermetallic alloys,. However, in-situ deformation tests revealed that dense dislocation storage can be achieved within FCC phases and dislocation walls were formed along phase boundaries. The unexpected strong interfaces are thought to be highly related to the chemically disordered distribution of multiple solution atoms at phase boundaries as well as in the matrix of HEAs. Particularly, an ultra-thin segregation zone of randomly distributed Cr atoms, typically less than 2 nm in width (Fig. 3b and S4), was detected near the phase boundary without forming complex intermetallic compounds, which were intrinsically brittle and would lead to stress concentration. This value is relatively high for metals,, and may imply a propensity for localized cohesive failure or fracture at the boundaries. Grain boundary decohesion has been recently shown to occur readily for this alloy due to segregation and nanoclustering of Cr, Ni and Mn at elevated temperature, and these failures typically originate along HAGBs and at triple junctions. In the present work there is no significant evidence of grain boundary segregation, and this is reasonable as a negligible increase in temperature is expected for these sliding conditions. This suggests that this alloy may also be prone to grain boundary decohesion without significant segregation and phase separation, i.e., when it is a solid solution.
